title: Coroner tells inquest jurors to rule homicide
article: The coroner's jury examining the shooting death of Keldon McMillan could have ruled it a suicide, the lawyer representing city police argued Thursday.

"I think the option of suicide should have been left for the jury to consider," Barry Rossman told presiding coroner Doug Kovach after jurors left a Queen's Bench courtroom to begin their deliberations.

During closing remarks, Kovach said homicide was the only conclusion open to jurors when deciding how McMillan died. In the context of a coroner's inquest, homicide doesn't imply wrongdoing. It means the death was caused by another human being, and not by accident, suicide, natural causes or undetermined means.
Kovach overruled Rossman's objection, saying the evidence didn't support a suicide finding.
McMillan, 33, died in a field off Highway 41 about seven kilometres south of Wakaw on May 20, 2001, after leading city police and RCMP on a high-speed chase from his home in northeast Saskatoon.

His business was in jeopardy, his wife had left him and there was evidence he had ingested cocaine and alcohol before the incident. Witnesses have testified he'd been talking about suicide for weeks and had warned of a shootout if police were called.
The jury's main task was to make recommendations aimed at preventing a similar death. In the end, jurors adopted three recommendations.

They suggested Saskatoon police add more RCMP radios to their cruisers, so officers are not cut off from communications when pursuing a vehicle outside the city. That did not appear to be a problem during the McMillan chase, because the city's canine units also have RCMP radios. The jury also recommended city police keep records of information given to officers during "parade" at the start of their shifts.

Jurors also recommended city police continue to study the idea of adding "tasers" -- devices used to temporarily paralyse suspects -- to their arsenal. The experts who testified Thursday said McMillan was too far away from police, and presented too much of an imminent threat, to make that option feasible.
